newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Sandoz to buy German drug maker for $416 million.
newsitem.headline: Sandoz to buy German drug maker for $416 million.

text.p: The Swiss drug maker Sandoz AG said Tuesday it agreed to buy Azupharma GmbH, Germany's third-largest generic drug company, for 640 million marks ($416 million) from Gehe AG of Germany.

The acquisition will help boost Sandoz's generic drug business, which is the stated aim of the man who will head Novartis Inc., the Swiss pharmaceuticals company to be formed from the merger of Sandoz AG and Ciba-Geigy AG.

"Buying a company which has an important position as No. 3 in Germany, which is the second-largest generics market in the world, puts us in a position where we will be becoming the No. 1 company in generics worldwide," Daniel Vasella, the designated head of Novartis, said after the deal was announced.
The merger of Sandoz and Ciba-Geigy has been approved by European regulators and is awaiting action by U.S. authorities.
For Gehe, a drug wholesaler, the sale of Azupharma and other manufacturing units will allow it to concentrate on its global wholesale business.
Both Sandoz and Ciba-Geigy already have big operations in generic drugs, which are not protected by patents and thus face fierce competition.
Sandoz specialises in bulk manufacturing, especially of antibiotics, while Ciba-Geigy's focus was on retail generics.
Combined with Azupharma, the companies' sales of generic drugs would total about 1.4 billion Swiss francs ($1.11 billion) a year, a company spokesman said.
Vasella noted that this was small compared with volumes in branded patented drugs, but said worldwide demand for generic drugs was growing at a rapid rate of almost 11 percent a year.
"I don't see any reason why increases in generics' growth should slow down significantly," he said.

"It is an industry which, under the auspices of health care cost containment, which is a worldwide phenomenon, will continue to play a very important role. It is in itself growing faster than the branded pharmaceutical market."
He said Azupharma was attractive in part because Gehe was getting out of the drugs manufacturing business and was looking to sell its operations in that field.

In its announcement in Frankfurt, Gehe also said it would sell its French unit GNR-pharma S.A. to a unit of Germany's BASF AG, and its Aliud Pharma GmbH & Co. KG and Allphamed mbH units, though it did not name buyers for the latter two.

Last summer, Gehe sold a 75 percent stake in its eastern German Jenapharm GmbH manufacturing unit for 500 million marks ($325 million) to Schering AG, the world's largest maker of oral contraceptives.
Based in Gerlingen near Stuttgart, Azupharma employs 440 people and had sales of 222 million marks ($145 million) in 1995. Branded generics account for 80 percent of sales.

Vasella said during the telephone interview that he was confident margins on generic products could be kept "significantly" above the 5 percent to 6 percent common in the United States, but he did not elaborate.

Generics will always play a subordinate role for Novartis's paharmaceutical division, Vasella made clear. "It is not an alternative to the research- and innovation-led part of the business. It is a complement and not a replacement," he said.
